subject: pe
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: According to the World Health Organisation, health is best defined as which of the following?
options: A state of complete physical, mental and social wellbeing, not merely the absence of disease
The ability to run, jump and throw without becoming tired
Having a body mass index below 25 and a normal resting heart rate
Being free from any injury or physical pain
questions.explain: The WHO defines health as complete physical, mental and social wellbeing, not simply the absence of illness or infirmity.

questions.q: Which of the following is an example of PHYSICAL wellbeing?
options: A reduced risk of illness and the ability to carry out everyday tasks
Feeling less stressed and more relaxed
Making new friends through a sports club
Feeling a sense of belonging within a team
questions.explain: Physical wellbeing includes improved fitness, a healthy weight and a reduced risk of illness so daily tasks can be performed.

questions.q: How does regular physical activity most directly improve a performer's EMOTIONAL wellbeing?
options: It releases feel-good hormones such as serotonin, reducing stress and improving mood
It increases muscle size so more everyday tasks can be completed
It creates opportunities to cooperate and socialise with others
It lowers resting heart rate and blood pressure
questions.explain: Exercise triggers the release of feel-good hormones that lower stress and lift mood, boosting emotional wellbeing.

questions.q: Which statement best describes a benefit to SOCIAL wellbeing from taking part in sport?
options: The chance to meet people, make friends and cooperate with others
A reduced risk of coronary heart disease
An improved ability to control emotions and cope with stress
A healthier body weight and better posture
questions.explain: Social wellbeing is improved through opportunities to mix with others, make friends and work cooperatively.

questions.q: Sam joins a five-a-side football league after work. He says he now feels part of a group and looks forward to seeing his teammates. Which type of wellbeing is Sam describing?
options: Social wellbeing
Physical wellbeing
Emotional wellbeing only
Nutritional wellbeing
questions.explain: Feeling part of a group and enjoying the company of teammates is a benefit to social wellbeing.

questions.q: A sedentary lifestyle is best defined as one that involves:
options: Little or no physical activity
A diet high in saturated fat
Regular high-intensity training
Frequent competitive sport
questions.explain: A sedentary lifestyle is one with irregular or no physical activity.

questions.q: Which of the following is a likely consequence of a sedentary lifestyle?
options: Weight gain leading to obesity
Increased flexibility
A lower resting heart rate
Improved cardiovascular endurance
questions.explain: Reduced activity means fewer calories are used, so excess energy is stored as fat, increasing the risk of obesity.

questions.q: Why does a sedentary lifestyle increase the risk of coronary heart disease?
options: Inactivity and weight gain raise blood pressure and fatty deposits that can block the coronary arteries
Inactivity strengthens the heart muscle too quickly
A lack of exercise increases the number of red blood cells
Sitting still lowers cholesterol in the bloodstream
questions.explain: Inactivity contributes to raised blood pressure and fatty build-up in the arteries, which can restrict blood flow to the heart.

questions.q: A doctor tells an inactive, overweight patient they are at greater risk of type 2 diabetes, high blood pressure and heart disease. These are all examples of:
options: Consequences of a sedentary lifestyle
Benefits of carbo-loading
Components of a balanced diet
Signs of good physical wellbeing
questions.explain: Type 2 diabetes, hypertension and heart disease are all health risks linked to a sedentary lifestyle.

questions.q: Which list correctly gives the three MACRONUTRIENTS?
options: Carbohydrates, fats and proteins
Vitamins, minerals and fibre
Water, fibre and vitamins
Calcium, iron and sodium
questions.explain: The macronutrients, needed in large amounts, are carbohydrates, fats and proteins.

questions.q: What is the main function of PROTEIN in the diet of a performer?
options: Growth and repair of muscle tissue
The body's main source of quick energy
Insulation and protection of vital organs
Aiding digestion and preventing constipation
questions.explain: Protein is primarily needed for the growth and repair of muscles and other body tissues.

questions.q: Carbohydrates are important in a performer's diet mainly because they:
options: Are the body's main source of energy
Are needed for the growth and repair of tissue
Provide insulation to keep the body warm
Carry fat-soluble vitamins around the body
questions.explain: Carbohydrates are the body's primary and preferred source of energy for exercise.

questions.q: Why might a marathon runner carry out carbo-loading in the days before a race?
options: To maximise glycogen stores in the muscles and delay fatigue
To increase muscle mass for greater strength
To reduce their body's need for water during the race
To lower their percentage of body fat quickly
questions.explain: Carbo-loading increases stored muscle glycogen, providing more energy for endurance events and delaying fatigue.

questions.q: Which of the following best represents the proportions of a balanced diet?
options: Around 55% carbohydrate, 30% fat and 15% protein
Around 55% fat, 30% protein and 15% carbohydrate
Around 55% protein, 30% carbohydrate and 15% fat
Around equal thirds of carbohydrate, fat and protein
questions.explain: A balanced diet is made up largely of carbohydrate, with smaller proportions of fat and protein.

questions.q: How does dehydration reduce a performer's ability to exercise effectively?
options: The blood thickens, so the heart must work harder and the performer tires more quickly
The muscles gain too much glycogen and become stiff
The body stores extra fat to replace lost water
Reaction time improves but strength is lost
questions.explain: Losing water thickens the blood, making the heart work harder and causing earlier fatigue and reduced performance.

questions.q: Which of these is a key function of WATER in the body?
options: Transporting nutrients and helping to regulate body temperature
Providing the main long-term store of energy
Growth and repair of muscle tissue
Protecting vital organs from impact
questions.explain: Water transports nutrients, removes waste and helps regulate body temperature, preventing dehydration.

questions.q: Although often linked to weight gain, why are some FATS still important in a performer's diet?
options: They provide a store of energy and help insulate and protect organs
They are the fastest source of energy during sprinting
They are needed for the growth and repair of muscle
They prevent constipation by aiding digestion
questions.explain: Fats provide an energy store, insulate the body and cushion vital organs, so some fat is needed in the diet.

questions.q: A rugby player wants to increase muscle size during a strength training programme. Which dietary change is most appropriate?
options: Increasing protein intake to support muscle growth and repair
Increasing saturated fat intake for insulation
Reducing water intake before every session
Removing all carbohydrate from the diet
questions.explain: Because protein is needed for muscle growth and repair, a slightly higher protein intake supports gains from strength training.

questions.q: The term obesity is used to describe a person who is:
options: Overfat to the extent that it seriously affects their health
Slightly above their ideal body weight
Carrying a large amount of muscle mass
Unable to complete an endurance event
questions.explain: Obesity describes carrying so much excess body fat that health is seriously impaired, a common consequence of a sedentary lifestyle.

questions.q: A teenager spends most of their free time sitting and gaming, and reports poor sleep, low mood and lethargy. These effects are best described as:
options: Consequences of a sedentary lifestyle on emotional and physical wellbeing
Signs of successful carbo-loading
Benefits of a balanced diet
Improvements to social wellbeing
questions.explain: Poor sleep, low mood and lethargy are wellbeing consequences commonly linked to an inactive, sedentary lifestyle.

specSource: OCR GCSE (9–1) PE & Sport Science (J587) specification; Health, Fitness and Well-being
